tagline: An eighth-century country prophet's indictment of Jerusalem's rulers for injustice, set beside promises of a coming ruler from Bethlehem and a God who delights in mercy.
overview:
Micah came from Moresheth, a small town in the foothills southwest of Jerusalem, and preached during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, in the second half of the eighth century BC. He was a contemporary of Isaiah, and he watched the Assyrian empire destroy the northern kingdom of Israel and then invade Judah. His book moves back and forth between judgment and hope. He charges the leaders of Jerusalem and Samaria with seizing land, perverting justice for bribes, and preaching comfort for pay, and he warns that Samaria will become rubble and that even Zion will be plowed like a field.

Yet each section of the book also turns toward hope. God will gather a remnant like a shepherd gathering sheep. In the last days the nations will stream to the mountain of the LORD to learn his ways, and swords will be beaten into plowshares (4:1-3, a passage that also appears in Isaiah 2:2-4). A ruler will come from little Bethlehem whose origins are from of old (5:2). In a courtroom scene God summarizes what he asks of his people: to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with God (6:8). The book ends with a hymn that plays on Micah's own name, which means who is like the LORD: no God is like the one who pardons iniquity and delights in loving devotion.

Micah matters because it joins two things that are often separated: a fierce concern for how the powerful treat the weak, and a deep hope rooted in God's faithfulness to his promises. Its words were remembered for a century (Jeremiah 26:18 quotes Micah 3:12), and its promise about Bethlehem was cited when wise men came looking for a newborn king (Matthew 2:5-6).
author:
The book is attributed to "Micah the Moreshite" (1:1), a prophet from Moresheth-gath (1:14) in the Shephelah, the lowland hill country between Judah's central mountains and the coastal plain. He is not called the son of anyone, and he is sometimes thought to have been a man of the countryside rather than of Jerusalem's elite, which may explain his anger at landlords who swallowed up small farms. Jeremiah 26:18 confirms that a prophet named Micah of Moresheth preached in Hezekiah's day and quotes his warning about Zion.

Scholars agree that much of chapters 1 to 3 comes from Micah himself. Views differ on the rest. Many critical scholars think chapters 4 to 7, or parts of them, were added by later editors during or after the exile, pointing to passages such as 4:10 (which names Babylon) and 7:8-20 (which seems to presuppose a ruined Jerusalem). Other scholars hold that the whole book, or most of it, goes back to Micah, arguing that eighth-century prophets could and did speak of both judgment and restoration, and that Babylon was already a restless power in Hezekiah's time.
date: Micah 1:1 places his ministry in the reigns of Jotham (about 750 to 735 BC, including a period as co-regent), Ahaz (about 735 to 715 BC), and Hezekiah (about 715 to 686 BC). Micah 1:6 speaks of Samaria's coming destruction, so at least that oracle comes before 722 BC, when Samaria fell to Assyria. Jeremiah 26:18 places his warning about Jerusalem in Hezekiah's reign, and the disaster sweeping toward Jerusalem in 1:10-16 fits the Assyrian invasion of Judah under Sennacherib in 701 BC. A ministry from about 740 to about 700 BC is a common estimate. Those who see later additions date them to the exile or the period after it.
setting:
The Assyrian empire dominated Micah's world. Tiglath-pileser III (about 745 to 727 BC) turned Assyria into an empire that deported conquered peoples. His successors besieged and destroyed Samaria in 722 BC, ending the northern kingdom. In 701 BC Sennacherib invaded Judah, captured many of its fortified towns, and besieged Jerusalem, which was spared (2 Kings 18-19, Isaiah 36-37). Sennacherib's palace at Nineveh was decorated with carved reliefs of his siege of Lachish, one of the towns Micah names (1:13); those reliefs are now in the British Museum. Many of the towns in Micah 1:10-16 lay in the Shephelah near his home, directly in the invader's path.

Inside Judah, the eighth century had brought wealth to some and loss to many. Land was supposed to stay within families as an inheritance from God (Leviticus 25, 1 Kings 21), but powerful men accumulated estates by debt, pressure, and corrupt courts. Isaiah, Micah's contemporary in Jerusalem, condemned the same practice: woe to those who add house to house and field to field (Isaiah 5:8).
purpose: Micah preached to Judah and Jerusalem, and first of all to their rulers, priests, and prophets, calling them to account for injustice and false security. He wanted them to see that the Assyrian threat was God's judgment on their sin, not a random event, and that their confidence that "the LORD is among us" would not protect them while they robbed the poor. At the same time, the book in its final form was preserved for generations who had seen that judgment fall, and it assured them that God would gather a remnant, raise up a faithful ruler, and keep the promises he swore to Abraham and Jacob (7:20). Jeremiah 26:18-19 records that Hezekiah heeded Micah's warning and that the disaster was delayed, which shows how later readers understood the purpose of his preaching: to bring repentance.
story: Micah preached during the years covered by 2 Kings 15-20 and 2 Chronicles 27-32, when Samaria fell and Jerusalem survived Sennacherib's siege. He was a contemporary of Isaiah in Judah and, early on, of Hosea in Israel; Amos had preached a little before him. In the canon Micah stands sixth among the twelve Minor Prophets, after Jonah and before Nahum, a book about the fall of Nineveh. Micah's promises look beyond his own time to the Babylonian exile, the return, and a coming ruler of David's line, and they feed directly into the New Testament's account of Jesus' birth in Bethlehem.
christ:
The best known link is Micah 5:2, which promises a ruler from Bethlehem Ephrathah, small among the clans of Judah, whose origins are from ancient times. When Herod asked where the Messiah was to be born, the chief priests and scribes answered from this verse (Matthew 2:5-6), and John 7:42 shows that people in Jesus' day expected the Messiah to come from Bethlehem. Micah 5:4 adds that this ruler will shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD, and Jesus called himself the good shepherd (John 10).

Other links are thematic. The vision of nations streaming to Zion to learn God's ways (4:1-3) finds a beginning in the gospel going out from Jerusalem to the nations (Luke 24:47, Acts 1:8). Micah 7:6, about a man's enemies being the members of his own household, is quoted by Jesus in Matthew 10:35-36. And the closing hymn to a God who pardons iniquity and casts sins into the depths of the sea is fulfilled, in Christian reading, in the forgiveness won by Christ.
reading:
Micah is prophetic poetry, compressed and vivid. The book is commonly divided into three cycles, each opening with the command "Hear" (1:2, 3:1, 6:1) and each moving from judgment to hope. Watch for wordplay, especially in 1:10-16, where the names of towns are turned into puns about their fate. Watch for the courtroom scene of chapter 6, where God brings a lawsuit against his people and calls the mountains as witnesses.

Two cautions help. First, Micah's hope passages are not a denial of his warnings; the book holds both, and the reader should not flatten it into only doom or only comfort. Second, Micah 6:8 is often quoted alone as a summary of religion without God's grace. In context it answers a people trying to buy God's favor with offerings, and it comes from a God who has already redeemed them from Egypt (6:4). It is a description of the life of a redeemed people, not a ladder to earn redemption.

structure.title: First cycle: judgment on Samaria and Judah, then a remnant gathered
structure.summary: God comes in judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem; the towns of the Shephelah mourn; land-grabbers are condemned. The cycle ends with the LORD gathering the remnant like sheep.

structure.title: Second cycle: corrupt leaders, then a coming ruler
structure.summary: Rulers, prophets, and priests are indicted and Zion's fall is announced. Then the mountain of the LORD is raised, the scattered are gathered, and a ruler comes from Bethlehem.

structure.title: Third cycle: God's lawsuit, then his unmatched mercy
structure.summary: God brings a case against his people and states what he requires. Micah laments the corruption of society, then waits for God and ends with a hymn to the God who pardons.

themes.title: Justice for the powerless
themes.body: Micah's harshest words are for those with power who use it to take fields, houses, and inheritances from ordinary families (2:1-2), for judges who take bribes, and for leaders who treat the people like meat for the pot (3:1-3). For Micah, injustice is not a side issue to worship; it is the reason worship has become offensive to God.

themes.title: False security
themes.body: Jerusalem's leaders said, "Is not the LORD among us? No disaster can come upon us" (3:11). Micah answers that God's presence is not a guarantee for those who defy him. Temple, priesthood, and prophets bought for pay cannot protect a city built with bloodshed.

themes.title: The remnant and the shepherd
themes.body: Again and again Micah pictures God as a shepherd who gathers the lame, the outcast, and the scattered (2:12, 4:6-7, 7:14), and a coming ruler who shepherds in the LORD's strength (5:4). Judgment is not God's last word; a remnant will be gathered and restored.

themes.title: The nations and Zion
themes.body: Micah sees a day when the nations will come to God's mountain to learn his ways and will abandon war (4:1-4). The same book also speaks of the nations' judgment. God's rule extends to all peoples, both in justice and in blessing.

themes.title: Who is like the LORD?
themes.body: The book closes by playing on Micah's name: no God is like the one who pardons iniquity, does not retain his anger forever, and delights in loving devotion (7:18). The final ground of hope is God's own character and his oath to Abraham and Jacob.

keyChapters.why: Micah's attack on those who seize land and inheritances, and his first promise of a gathered remnant.
The indictment of rulers, priests, and prophets and the warning that Zion will be plowed like a field, remembered a century later in Jeremiah 26:18.
The nations stream to the mountain of the LORD and beat swords into plowshares, the same vision found in Isaiah 2:2-4.
The promise of a ruler from Bethlehem, cited in Matthew 2:6.
God's lawsuit against his people and the summary of what he requires: justice, mercy, and humble walking with God.
The book's closing hymn to the God who pardons and keeps his promises to Abraham and Jacob.
